note: W1-LIBRARY round 3. Two jobs in one file. The Articles close book-budget X3: game/data/quests/faction-wet-ledger.json names `book_articles_of_the_wet_ledger` as the book channel for two reveals (rev_the_article on Q-LEDG-14, rev_the_bound_copy on Q-LEDG-15) and no such book existed on disk, so both reveals were unreachable. The eighth article is the two-house article the quest turns on, and it is in the text as a constitutional clause among ten others, with no reference to any quest, objective or player. The three volumes of Ganeeth-Ei are the library's fifth multi-volume series and its human spine: the same auxiliary at 31, 47 and 61, each volume disagreeing with the one before it, the third retracting a claim that the depot returns actually support. Nothing corrects any of the three.

books.title: The Articles of the Wet Ledger, Being the Founding Papers of the Company of Underwriters of the Topal Trade, With the Amendments to Date
books.author: engrossed at Archon by hands unnamed; the marginal notes are by four successive clerks of the table over ninety years
books.unreliability: A constitution, which is to say a document that is entirely true and is not read. Everything in it is in force. Four of the articles have not been cited at the table in living memory, and the clerks' marginalia record, without any apparent alarm, the exact points at which the table stopped reading each one.
books.text:
THE ARTICLES OF THE COMPANY OF UNDERWRITERS OF THE TOPAL TRADE, COMMONLY THE WET LEDGER.

*Engrossed at Archon. To be read entire at the first water-call of each year, in the hearing of the table, by the clerk.*

*(Marginal note, first clerk's hand:* "Read entire at the water-call, 3E 344, 3E 345, 3E 346. Took the better part of a morning each time and the fourth seat complained." *)*

**ARTICLE THE FIRST. OF WHAT THE COMPANY IS.**

The Company is not a house, not a guild, and not a chartered body of the Empire. It is an agreement among persons who insure cargo against water, and it exists because a keel that goes down between Lilmoth and Archon ruins one merchant entire and ruins twelve merchants a little, and twelve merchants may be ruined a little for a very long time.

The Company owns nothing. It holds a book. The book is the Company.

**ARTICLE THE SECOND. OF THE TABLE.**

The table shall be of five seats and no more and no fewer.

The five seats are: the first chair, which speaks for the book; the second, for the Archon wharf; the third, for the Lilmoth wharf; the fourth, for the upriver trade; and the fifth, for the underwriters who hold no wharf at all.

No seat is a person. A seat is an interest, and the person in it holds it for that interest and not for themselves, and a person who has forgotten this is to be reminded by the clerk, aloud, at the table.

*(Second clerk's hand:* "The fifth has been vacant or held by proxy since 3E 371. I have entered it as vacant. I have been told to enter it as held." *)*

**ARTICLE THE THIRD. OF THE FIRST CHAIR.**

The first chair is chosen by the four other seats, unanimously, and serves until death, resignation, or the operation of the eighth article.

The first chair may veto any motion of the table once. A veto so exercised stands for one full year and may then be overturned by the four seats together, and by no lesser number, and the overturning shall be recorded in the book with the four names and the date.

*(Third clerk's hand:* "Overturned once in ninety years. 3E 420, the Dres seat. Four names entered. One of the four was Corvo the elder, who was buried at Archon in 3E 419." *)*

**ARTICLE THE FOURTH. OF THE WATER-CALL.**

Twice in the year, at the turn of the seasons, the table shall sit and shall call the water: which is to say shall set, for the following half-year, the rate at which the Company will insure each reach of the coast.

The call binds every member. A member who insures below the call outside the table is not a member and the book shall be struck through against their name in the presence of the table.

**ARTICLE THE FIFTH. OF THE BOOK.**

The clerk keeps it. The clerk is not of the table and may not vote and may not be dismissed except by the first chair alone.

Every entry in the book is to be made in the clerk's own hand at the table, in the hearing of the seats, and read back before the table rises. An entry made afterwards is not an entry.

*(Fourth clerk's hand:* "I have read every entry back for 19 years and the table has not listened for the last 12." *)*

**ARTICLE THE SIXTH. OF THE UPRIVER TRADE.**

The fourth seat speaks for cargo that has come down a river, and cargo that has come down a river is not the same risk as cargo that has come along a coast, and the Company was founded on that distinction and shall not abandon it.

Nothing that walks is cargo. The Company does not underwrite a keel that carries persons under lease, whatever the lease says, and a member who brings such a risk to the table shall be refused, and the refusal entered.

*(Second clerk's hand:* "Cited at the table three times: 3E 358, 3E 371, 3E 402. Not cited since." *)*

**ARTICLE THE SEVENTH. OF PROXIES.**

A seat that is unable to attend may lodge a proxy with the clerk, in writing, naming the person and the motion.

A proxy is good for one sitting. A standing proxy is good for one year and must be renewed at a water-call in person by the seat that lodged it, and a standing proxy that has not been so renewed is void from the day it should have been renewed and not from the day the clerk notices.

*(Fourth clerk's hand, in a different ink:* "Read the last clause again. Then go and look at the fourth seat's proxy." *)*

**ARTICLE THE EIGHTH. OF THE FALLING VACANT OF THE FIRST CHAIR.**

The first chair falls vacant upon the death or resignation of the holder.

The first chair also falls vacant, without death and without resignation, when two of the wharf seats — being the second and the third — declare together, at a water-call, in the hearing of the table, that the book has been kept against the interest of the wharves.

Such a declaration requires both wharf seats and neither may be exercised by proxy. It requires no other seat and it may not be vetoed, the veto of the third article being a veto upon motions of the table and this being no motion of the table.

The declaration shall be entered in the book by the clerk in the clerk's own hand and read back, and upon the reading back the chair is vacant.

*(First clerk's hand:* "The two-house article. Put in at the founding at the insistence of the Lilmoth wharf, which did not trust Archon, and agreed to by Archon, which did not trust Lilmoth." *)*

*(Third clerk's hand, much later:* "Never used." *)*

*(Fourth clerk's hand:* "Never used, and I have been asked twice this year by seats of this table how a first chair may be removed, and both times I have been asked as though it were a question with no answer, and both times I have said nothing, because a clerk answers what is put to him and neither of them put it to me." *)*

**ARTICLE THE NINTH. OF THE CLOSING OF A REACH.**

The table may declare a reach of the coast uninsurable. Such a declaration shuts the reach as surely as a chain across it, since no keel will sail uninsured and no factor will lade one.

This power shall be used against water and against nothing else.

*(Fourth clerk's hand:* "Used four times. Three against water." *)*

**ARTICLE THE TENTH. OF THE WHARF THAT IS NOT A SEAT.**

Where a wharf keeps its own book and holds its own risk and has done so for seven years unbroken, that wharf shall be counted at the water-call, and its count shall stand with the seats.

*(Second clerk's hand:* "This has never been given effect. I raised it in 3E 369 and was told the wharves in question were not of the Company. The article does not say they must be." *)*

*(Fourth clerk's hand:* "Raised again. Same answer. Same article." *)*

**ARTICLE THE ELEVENTH. OF AMENDMENT.**

These articles may be amended by the table, unanimously, at a water-call, and no amendment shall be made in the same sitting in which it is first proposed.

An article that is struck out is to be struck through and left legible, with the date and the five names, so that whoever comes after may see what the Company thought it could do without.

*(Fourth clerk's hand, at the foot of the last leaf:* "Nothing has ever been struck out. Four things have been forgotten, which is cheaper." *)*

---

**SCHEDULE. OF THE WATER-CALLS SINCE THE FOUNDING, AS THE CLERKS HAVE ENTERED THEM AT THE HEAD OF EACH YEAR'S BOOK.**

*(Kept at the front of the current book and copied forward by each clerk from the last. The fourth clerk has added the right-hand column and it is not part of the Articles.)*

3E 344. First water-call. Five seats sat. Rates set for 6 reaches. *(All 5 present in person.)*

3E 358. Article the Sixth cited by the third seat against a lading out of Blackrose. Risk refused. Refusal entered. *(The first time.)*

3E 369. Article the Tenth raised by the clerk. Not given effect. *(By the clerk, not by a seat. The clerk was thanked.)*

3E 371. Article the Sixth cited by the first chair. Risk refused. The fifth seat vacant from this call. *(Both entries in the same sitting, which the third clerk has marked with a line in the margin and no comment.)*

3E 388. The Archon and Lilmoth wharves in dispute over a salvage. Settled by the table. *(The only time in 90 years the two wharf seats have been on opposite sides of anything, and the eighth article requires them to act together.)*

3E 402. Article the Sixth cited by the second seat. Risk refused. *(The last time.)*

3E 411. Reach closed under the ninth article. Against water. *(A wreck.)*

3E 414. Reach closed under the ninth article. Against water. *(A wreck.)*

3E 419. Reach closed under the ninth article. Against water. *(A wreck.)*

3E 420. The Dres seat. The first chair's veto overturned by four seats. Four names entered. *(The fourth closure under the ninth article was in this year and it was not against water, and it is not in this schedule, and I have looked for it in three books.)*

3E 421. Standing proxy on the fourth seat renewed. *(In person. The last time it was renewed in person.)*

3E 425. Rates set. *(The fourth seat by proxy, as in 422, 423 and 424.)*

---

*(A loose leaf in the fourth clerk's hand, kept between the last two leaves of the Articles, in the same ink as the marginalia:)*

I am going to write this once and put it where the Articles are and not in the book, because the book is read back and this is not fit to be read back.

I have been clerk for 19 years. In that time I have entered every word the table has said and I have not once been asked what I thought, and that is correct, and I have never resented it.

Three of the five seats have never read these Articles. I know this because I have watched them look for things in them.

The fourth seat's standing proxy has been void since 3E 422 by the plain words of the seventh article, and every motion carried on it since is standing on nothing, and I have entered every one of them because entering them is my office and refusing is not.

The eighth article has been on the first leaf of this book for 90 years.

I am not permitted to raise it. A clerk answers what is put to him.

It has been put to me.

books.title: Thirty Years in the Auxiliaries: Volume the First, Being the Years of Not Understanding
books.author: Ganeeth-Ei, auxiliary and then decurion, Ninth Cohort; written at 31 and printed at Gideon at his own cost
books.unreliability: Written by a proud young man who has been paid to be proud, and it reads like it, and the third volume says so. He believes the Cohort took him because he was good. The recruiting returns for that year, which he had not seen, took everyone who came.
books.text:
I was 17 and I walked to Gideon because a man at our landing said they were paying 6 drakes a month and I had never held 6 drakes.

VOLUME THE FIRST covers my first 9 years and I am writing it because a clerk at the depot told me it had never been done, and because I would like my mother to be able to read what I have been doing, and because I am proud and I do not intend to pretend otherwise in my own book.

WHAT THEY DID WITH ME.

They took my name down and looked at my hands and asked whether I could swim, and when I said we can all swim they wrote something and did not explain it, and I found out 3 years later that they write it on every one of us and it is the reason we get the water work.

Then they gave me a shortsword.

I want to say something about that sword because everything else in this volume comes out of it. It was a marsh-guard pattern — short, heavy at the belly, carried low on the left, and it is the sword the auxiliaries have carried on this coast since before there was a Cohort. It is not the garrison sword the Imperials carry. It is ours, and they issue it to us, and I did not think about that at all for 9 years.

Serjeant Brell put it in my hand and said: this is 3 things. It is a knife you can reach anything with, it is a lever, and it is a way of not having to think when you are frightened. He said: I am going to teach you the third one.

He did. That was the whole of my first year. One cut, thrown from the hip, from the carry, without looking, until I could do it asleep. Then the same cut coming back. Then a low thrust off the same footwork. He would not teach me anything else and I asked him every week and he said no, and I hated him, and by the end of the year I could do those 3 things when I was tired and cold and there was a serjeant shouting, and I have not needed a fourth thing in 9 years.

WHAT THE FIRST YEARS WERE ACTUALLY LIKE.

Wet. Boring. Very well fed.

I want the fed part in the book because the recruiting bills leave it out and it was the largest single fact of my early service. At home we ate what the season gave. In the Cohort I ate twice a day, every day, whatever the season was doing, and I put on a stone in my first 6 months and grew 2 inches at 18, and half the auxiliaries in my intake did the same, and when I went home on leave my mother cried and I did not understand why for a long time.

We marched. We stood in water. We escorted the salt carts to Thorn and back and nothing ever happened. In 4 years I drew my sword twice in earnest and both times it was against a drunk off a boat.

THE CHANNEL AT STORMHOLD, WHICH IS WHAT PEOPLE ASK ME ABOUT.

I was 22.

There is nothing clever to tell. Raiders came up the water stair at the third hour and the alarm went and we came down the lane in whatever we were sleeping in. There were 4 of us with swords and Brell had a shield and there was a fen lad from Blackrose with a greatsword who I did not know.

The fen lad went to the front of the lane and stood there and did not swing at anything for the first minute, and I remember being angry with him, and then I saw that not one of them could get past him and that he was not swinging because he had not needed to yet.

I was behind Brell and I did the thing I had been taught. Low carry, cut from the hip, come back. Over and over, into whatever was in the gap beside Brell's shield, without looking, because there was nothing to look at, because it was dark and there were too many arms.

It went on for as long as it took to get the boats off and I have no idea how long that was. One of the lads said an hour. It did not feel like an hour and it did not feel like a minute; it felt like nothing at all, and then it was over and I was sitting down and my hand would not open.

Brell came and prised my fingers off the grip one at a time and did not say anything about it, and then he said: good, and went away, and that is the only time in 9 years he has said it.

WHAT I THINK ABOUT ALL THIS.

I think I am lucky. I think the Cohort took me because I was quick and because I could swim and because Brell saw something in the yard, and I think a great many young ones from the landings could not have done it.

I think the province is better with us in it. The salt gets to Thorn. No raider takes the drying racks at Hollow-Reeds any more and the reason they do not is that there is a post at Hollow-Reeds and there is a post at Hollow-Reeds because I asked for one and was listened to.

And I think the people at home who say we are theirs and not ours have not been to a landing that has been burned.

THE PAY, FOR ANYONE THINKING OF COMING.

Six drakes the month when they take you. A file-leader gets 12. A decurion gets 20, which I have been since the spring, and which the clerk tells me makes me the third Argonian decurion in the Ninth and the youngest.

They stop 2 for the kit and 1 for the burial fund and you get the burial fund back at 20 years, and I have never met anyone who got it back.

My mother has the address at the depot. She writes.

books.title: Thirty Years in the Auxiliaries: Volume the Second, Being the Years of the Work Itself
books.author: Ganeeth-Ei, decurion and then serjeant, Ninth Cohort; written at 47 and not printed until after the third volume
books.unreliability: The middle volume of a memoir, written by a man in the middle of a career, and it is a professional's book that will not go near the two things the first and third volumes are both about. He notices this himself, once, and calls it having a job.
books.text:
I wrote the first volume at 31. It has been read out at depots. I am told recruits laugh at it.

I am 47. I have been a serjeant for 9 years. I have very little to say and I am going to say it carefully.

WHAT THE WORK IS.

Escort. Patrol. Post. Count. Burial. In that order by hours spent.

Escort is salt to Thorn. Iron to Blackrose. The Assize clerk's boat when a clerk of the Assize goes anywhere. And the lease convoys, which I will come to.

Patrol is the road between the posts in daylight. Four men and a poler. In 16 years of patrolling I have found 3 bodies, 22 abandoned boats, one very frightened Cyrodiil surveyor 9 miles from where he thought he was, and no enemy at all. Ever.

Post is standing at a place so that people can see a soldier is standing at it. It is the largest part of the work. It is what the Cohort actually does. No book about the Legion mentions it.

Count is stores. I am good at it. It has done more for my rank than anything I have done with a sword.

Burial is burial. We do our own. We do the ones the river brings. There is a form.

WHAT I HAVE LEARNED ABOUT KEEPING MEN ALIVE.

This is the only useful part of the volume.

Water. Every hour. Whether they want it or not. Stand over the proud ones. I have lost 2 men in 16 years and neither was killed.

Boots off at every long halt. Feet dried. Feet looked at by me, personally. A serjeant who will not look at feet will be writing letters instead.

Do not let them sit down in wet kit. Standing rest, on the pole.

Feed them before you feed yourself. Eat last, visibly, every time. Never explain why.

Send the man who is frightened to fetch something. He will come back different. I do not know why this works. I have used it a hundred times.

And the one they do not teach. Know which of your men are from here and which are not. Give the local ones the ground. Give the outland ones the paper.

A Colovian recruit who is told to read a channel will drown a boat out of pride. An auxiliary from the landings who is told to keep the stores book will be short by the first month and ashamed for a year.

THE LEASE CONVOYS.

I have escorted 31 of them.

A lease convoy is a barge of leased labour. It goes from Blackrose down to the coast, under a paper signed by the Assize. Our part is to walk beside it. To see that nothing happens to it. Nothing has ever happened to any of mine.

The people on the barges are from the landings. Some of them are from my landing. On the 19th convoy there was a woman on the barge who knew my mother's name and used it.

I have thought about how to write this part for 6 years. Here is what I have decided to put down.

The lease is lawful. I have read one. The Assize signs it. The term is entered. There is a return date on the paper. I have been told by a clerk I trust that in his experience some of them come back.

I walk beside the barge. My orders are to see that nothing happens to it. If a man came out of the reeds to stop that barge I would stop him. I would be right to. I have 6 men whose mothers I have met, and a barge full of people who would be in the water inside a minute.

That is all true. I have said it to myself on 31 convoys.

I am 47. I am a serjeant of the Ninth Cohort. I have a burial fund and 3 years to go on the second engagement.

WHAT THIS VOLUME IS NOT ABOUT.

A clerk at the depot read the draft. He asked me why there is nothing in it about the first volume's opinions, and nothing about the convoys except the section above, which he called short.

I have thought about his question. The answer is that I have a job.

A man with 9 years to serve writes what a man with 9 years to serve can write. If that is a poor answer it is at least an honest one. I would rather put it in the book than pretend I had not been asked.

ONE THING I WILL SAY PLAINLY.

The recruits laugh at the first volume because of the part where I say the province is better with us in it.

They are right to laugh at how I said it. I was 31. I had been given a rank. I wrote like a man who had been given a rank.

I would still say a version of it. The salt gets to Thorn. There is a post at Hollow-Reeds. No raider has burned a landing on this stretch of coast in 22 years.

I would just not put an exclamation on the end of it now.

books.title: Thirty Years in the Auxiliaries: Volume the Third, Written After the Discharge, and Against the First
books.author: Ganeeth-Ei, formerly serjeant, Ninth Cohort, at his sister's house at Hollow-Reeds; written at 61 and printed by subscription
books.unreliability: He is now certain the first volume was propaganda and he is over-correcting. Two of the things he retracts were true. He cannot remember writing the passage he is most ashamed of and quotes it slightly wrong, and the misquotation is worse than the original, and nobody has told him.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Retracts the claim that no landing has been burned on that coast in twenty-two years, calling it a lie he was given. The depot returns support it. He has confused it with a different claim in the same paragraph, which was a lie.
books.text:
I am 61. I have been out 4 years. I am at my sister's house and I have my hands back, mostly, and I have read the first volume for the first time since I wrote it.

I would like to withdraw a great deal of it and there is no withdrawing it, because it has been read out at depots for 30 years and there are men in this province who joined because of it.

So this volume is the retraction, and I have paid for it myself, and 41 people have subscribed, and 9 of them are men I served with.

ON THE SWORD.

The first volume says they gave me a marsh-guard shortsword and that it is our sword and that they issue it to us, and I wrote that as though it were a kindness.

It is not a kindness. It is cheaper. A marsh pattern is made at Archon for 9 drakes and a garrison sword is shipped from Cyrodiil at 30, and every auxiliary in the Ninth carries the cheap one and every Imperial carries the other, and in 30 years I never once heard an officer say so, and in 30 years I never once worked it out.

The sword is a good sword. Brell taught me 3 things with it and they kept me alive and I have no complaint about the steel.

I have a complaint about a 17-year-old who was told the weapon was his people's heritage by a quartermaster who was doing his stores.

ON BEING TAKEN BECAUSE I WAS GOOD.

I wrote that the Cohort took me because I was quick and could swim and because Brell saw something in the yard.

I have since seen the recruiting return for that year. It is in the depot book at Gideon and any serjeant may look at it and I never did in 30 years.

They took 44 that year. Forty-four applied.

ON THE PART I AM MOST ASHAMED OF.

There is a passage near the end of the first volume where I say the people at home who call us theirs and not ours have not been to a landing that has been burned.

I have been asked about that sentence at 4 different depots by 4 different young ones and I gave the same proud answer every time.

Here is what I know now that I did not know at 31. The landing I was thinking of was burned by raiders off a boat, and the raiders were taking people, and the people they were taking were being sold north through a port that our own Assize licenses, and there was a Cohort post 9 miles away that did not go, and the reason it did not go is written in the day-book as *no orders*, and the man who did not give the orders was afterwards promoted, and I know his name, and I am not going to print it because his grandchildren are at Gideon.

So the sentence is true and it is the worst kind of true. Yes, they burned a landing. And we were 9 miles away with 40 men and a boat.

ON THE CONVOYS, WHICH THE SECOND VOLUME WOULD NOT DISCUSS.

I escorted 31 lease convoys and I wrote a page about it at 47 and the page says the lease is lawful and that I had 6 men whose mothers I had met.

Both true. Both a way of not finishing a sentence.

Here is the finished sentence. I walked beside 31 barges of people from the landings, going down to the coast, under a paper, and I would have stopped any man who tried to stop them, and on the 19th there was a woman who knew my mother's name.

I have thought about her for 42 years and I have never once written down what I said to her.

I said: I am sorry, aunt, I am on duty.

She said: I know you are.

That is the whole of it. She was not angry with me. Not one person on any of those barges was ever angry with me. And I would give the burial fund and the 30 years and both other volumes to have had her be angry with me.

ON THE BURIAL FUND.

They stop 1 drake a month for it and you get it back at 20 years.

I served 30. I asked for it at my discharge and was told it does not apply to the second engagement, and I said I had never been told that, and the clerk was embarrassed and looked and it is true, it is in the terms, and it has been in the terms since before I was born, and every auxiliary in the Ninth is paying it and I have never met one who got it back.

It is 360 drakes over 30 years. It is not the money. I want to be clear that it is not the money.

WHAT I WOULD SAY TO A YOUNG ONE NOW.

The same thing Brell said to me, because it is still the only true thing said to me in 30 years.

He put the sword in my hand and he said: I am going to teach you not to have to think when you are frightened.

He did. It works. It is the finest gift I was ever given and I have given it to perhaps 200 young ones since.

And the whole of my 61 years comes down to this: they teach you not to think when you are frightened, and then they arrange the rest of your life so that you are frightened, and the thinking never happens at all, and one day you are 57 and they hand you a paper and you go home and it starts.

Do not join. Or join, because 6 drakes is 6 drakes and my mother ate.

But read the recruiting return in your first month. It is in the depot book. Any serjeant may look at it.

*(Subscribers' list, 41 names, follows. Nine are entered with a rank and a cohort. Three are entered as "of the landings, no rank." The last name on the list is entered simply as "the woman from the nineteenth barge, if she is alive, paid for by the author.")*

ON WHAT I WILL NOT RETRACT, WHICH IS SHORTER THAN THE REST AND MATTERS MORE.

I have spent this volume taking things back and a man who takes everything back has written a book that means nothing.

So. Four things stand.

*Brell.* Everything I wrote about him at 31 was true and I would write it stronger now. He taught 3 things to a boy who could not read and the 3 things worked for 30 years, and he never once in 22 years took a drink from an Imperial officer in front of his own auxiliaries, and I did not understand why until I had my own file.

*The lads in my file.* I said 2 of them were better than me and knew it and did not say so. Still true. One of them is a serjeant at Archon and the other was killed at 24 in a boat, not in a fight, and I have never written his name down anywhere and I am not going to start.

*The stand at Stormhold.* I wrote it flat and short at 31 and every reader of the volume says that part is the best of it, and the reason it is flat and short is that it is the only part I did not decorate. I have nothing to add and nothing to take away.

*The post at Hollow-Reeds.* I asked for it and I was listened to and there has been a post there for 34 years. That is the one thing in 30 years of service that I can point at.

ON THE THING I HAVE BEEN AVOIDING FOR THREE VOLUMES.

A young one at the depot asked me last year, in front of people, whether I thought the Cohort was ours or theirs.

At 31 I would have said ours. At 47 I would have found something to do with the stores. At 61, in front of 9 people, I said I did not know, and then I sat down, and the young one was embarrassed for me.

Here is the answer I did not have that day.

It is theirs. The pay comes from Cyrodiil, the orders come from the Office, and on the day the Office wanted 31 barges walked down to the coast, 31 barges were walked down to the coast by people from the landings, and I was one of them.

And it is ours, because there are 400 of us in it and 40 Imperials, and because the salt gets to Thorn, and because when a landing on this coast is in trouble the people who come are people from the next landing wearing the Empire's boots.

Both. Not half and half. Entirely both, at the same time, all day, for 30 years, and the not being able to hold the two of them in your head is not a failure of thinking. It is what the arrangement is *for*. A province held by an Office in Cyrodiil could be argued with. A province held by 400 of its own children in Imperial boots cannot be argued with at all, least of all by them.

I would like a young one to read that sentence before they walk to Gideon rather than after, and that is the whole reason there is a third volume, and I have taken 61 years and 3 books to get to it and I could have said it in a paragraph.
